title: ssh: log in with a key
summary: Open a shell on another machine with a key pair, keep ~/.ssh private, and check the server is the right one.

scheme: private, stays here     your public key
text: ssh opens a shell on another machine, and everything on the way is encrypted.
- Log in with a key, not a password: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 makes the pair (the keys lesson explains how the two halves work).
- Give it a passphrase: it protects the private key if your laptop is stolen.
- ssh-copy-id you@backup.internal puts your public key in the server's authorized_keys.
~/.ssh/config gives a short name to a server, with its user and key.
- ssh backup now means all of that; scp and rsync read the same file.
- ssh -v shows what ssh tries, key after key: the first thing to read when a login fails.
ssh guards your keys, and refuses files with loose rights.
- A private key anyone but you can read or write: "Permissions 0644 ... are too open. This private key will be ignored."
- On the server, sshd ignores authorized_keys if others can write it, ~/.ssh or your home folder: someone could add their key.
- chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 on the private key fix it.

scheme: next times: same key? connect. other key?
text: The first time, ssh shows the server's fingerprint and asks you.
- Compare it with the one the admin gives you, another way (a chat, a wiki). Better: paste it instead of yes, and ssh accepts only if it matches.
- If the key changes later, ssh stops. Ask why first: a reinstalled server, or someone in the middle. Then run the ssh-keygen -R line the warning prints: it forgets only that server's old key.
- Never skip the check with StrictHostKeyChecking=no.
